questions.explanation: The binary search algorithm starts at the middle of a sorted data set and eliminates half of the data. This process repeats until the desired value is found or all elements have been eliminated.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes why binary search is often more efficient than linear search on sorted data?

questions.explanation: Binary search is often more efficient than linear search when applied to sorted data because it eliminates half the remaining data with each step, while linear search checks one element at a time.

options.D: A method of compressing code to reduce the number of lines in a program

questions.explanation: Procedural abstraction provides a name for a process and allows a procedure to be used only knowing what it does, not how it does it. This hides the implementation details from the user of the procedure.

questions.question: What is modularity in programming?

options.C: The process of converting a program to use fewer variables

questions.question: A programmer writes a procedure called calculateTax that computes sales tax. They use it in 10 different places in the program. If the tax rate changes, what is the main benefit of having used a procedure?

options.A: The program will automatically update all tax calculations without any changes
options.B: The programmer only needs to change the code in one place (the procedure definition) rather than in all 10 locations
options.C: The procedure will calculate the new tax rate automatically by reading from the internet
options.D: The programmer needs to delete and rewrite the entire program from scratch

questions.explanation: A procedural abstraction may extract shared features to generalize functionality instead of duplicating code. This allows for code reuse which helps manage complexity — when the logic changes, it only needs to be updated in one place.

questions.question: A programmer improves a sorting procedure to run twice as fast by using a better algorithm internally. Users of the procedure don't need to be notified of this change. Which principle does this demonstrate?

options.C: Modularity requires that all procedures be documented when changed
options.D: Selection, because the procedure now selects a better algorithm based on input size

questions.explanation: Using procedural abstraction allows programmers to change the internals of a procedure (to make it faster, more efficient, use less storage, etc.) without needing to notify users of the change as long as what the procedure does is preserved.

questions.question: A programmer writes the following two procedures: drawSquare10 that draws a square with side 10, and drawSquare50 that draws a square with side 50. She notices they are almost identical. What is the best approach to improve this code?

questions.explanation: Using parameters allows procedures to be generalized, enabling them to be reused with a range of input values or arguments. A procedural abstraction may extract shared features to generalize functionality instead of duplicating code.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains how procedural abstraction allows a solution to a large problem to be based on solutions to smaller subproblems?

options.B: By creating procedures to solve each subproblem, programmers can build a large solution from smaller, tested, reusable pieces
options.C: Procedural abstraction requires that all subproblems be solved before any procedure is written
options.D: Procedures automatically break large problems into subproblems without programmer intervention

questions.explanation: Procedural abstraction allows a solution to a large problem to be based on the solutions of smaller subproblems. This is accomplished by creating procedures to solve each of the subproblems.

questions.question: A programmer uses a procedure called sortList throughout their program without knowing exactly how it sorts — just that it produces a sorted list. Which principle does this demonstrate?

questions.question: Which of the following is a benefit of using procedural abstraction in a program?

questions.question: Which of the following best describes how using parameters makes procedures more general?

questions.question: Why is documentation for an API necessary?

options.A: Documentation makes the program run faster by providing optimization hints
options.B: Documentation for an API/library is necessary in understanding the behaviors provided by the API and how to use them
options.C: Documentation is required by law for all published software libraries
options.D: Documentation replaces the need to test programs that use the API

questions.explanation: Documentation for an API/library is necessary in understanding the behaviors provided by the API/library and how to use them. Without documentation, programmers cannot know what procedures are available or how to call them correctly.

questions.question: A programmer uses a math library that provides a sqrt() procedure without knowing how it calculates square roots internally. Which principle does this demonstrate?

options.A: Data abstraction, because the programmer is storing numbers in a library
options.B: Procedural abstraction, because the programmer uses the procedure knowing only what it does not how
options.C: Iteration, because calculating square roots involves repeated approximation
options.D: Selection, because the procedure selects the correct output for each input

questions.explanation: Using a library procedure demonstrates procedural abstraction — the programmer can use sqrt() knowing only what it does (calculates the square root) without needing to know how the internal algorithm works.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes where existing code segments used in a program can come from?

options.A: Only from internal sources within the same program
options.B: Only from external libraries written by other companies
options.C: From internal or external sources such as libraries or previously written code
options.D: Only from code that the programmer wrote themselves in previous projects

questions.explanation: Existing code segments can come from internal or external sources, such as libraries or previously written code. Both sources can provide useful building blocks for new programs.

questions.question: A web developer uses a library to handle user authentication. The library is updated by its creators and becomes more secure. The developer updates to the new version. What benefit does using a library provide here?

options.A: The developer automatically knows about every security improvement made to the library
options.B: The developer can improve the security of their app by updating one library rather than rewriting all authentication code from scratch
options.C: The library prevents any security vulnerabilities from occurring in the developer's program
options.D: The library's documentation becomes unnecessary after the update

questions.explanation: The use of libraries simplifies the task of creating complex programs. When a library improves, developers who use it benefit from those improvements by simply updating to the new version rather than rewriting complex code.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of using software libraries?

options.A: Libraries simplify the task of creating complex programs
options.B: Libraries provide pre-written, tested procedures that can be reused
options.C: Libraries guarantee that programs using them will be free of all bugs
options.D: Libraries allow programmers to leverage existing code without writing it from scratch

questions.explanation: Libraries simplify program creation and provide pre-written, tested procedures, but they do not guarantee that programs using them will be bug-free. Bugs can still exist in how a programmer uses the library, even if the library itself is correct.

questions.question: A programmer wants to use a procedure from a library. They look up the API documentation. What information would they expect to find there?

options.A: The complete source code of every procedure in the library
options.B: The names of the programmers who wrote the library
options.C: Information about how the procedures behave and how to use them including parameters and return values
options.D: Performance benchmarks comparing the library to all competitor libraries

questions.explanation: Documentation for an API/library is necessary in understanding the behaviors provided by the API/library and how to use them. This includes what procedures are available, what parameters they accept, and what they return.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains why software libraries are important for managing complexity in large programs?

options.A: Libraries hide all the complexity from the programmer so they never need to understand algorithms
options.B: Libraries provide reusable, tested procedures that allow programmers to build complex programs without implementing every component from scratch
options.C: Libraries automatically generate the entire program based on a description of what it should do
options.D: Libraries replace the need for procedural abstraction and modularity

questions.explanation: The use of libraries simplifies the task of creating complex programs by providing pre-written, tested procedures. This allows programmers to focus on solving the unique aspects of their problem rather than reimplementing common functionality.

questions.question: A programmer is building a mapping application. She uses a maps API that provides procedures for displaying maps, getting directions, and finding locations. Which of the following best describes the relationship between the API and the procedures?

options.A: The API is a procedure and the procedures are variables
options.B: The API specifies how the procedures in the library behave and can be used, while the library contains the actual procedures
options.C: The API is the same thing as a procedure and both terms mean the same thing
options.D: The API replaces the procedures and programmers use the API directly instead

questions.explanation: APIs are specifications for how the procedures in a library behave and can be used. The API documentation tells programmers what procedures exist and how to call them, while the library contains the actual implementations.

questions.question: Two programmers are building different apps. Both apps need to process credit card payments. Instead of each writing their own payment code, both use the same payment processing library. Which concept does this demonstrate?

options.A: Data abstraction, because payment data is stored in a list
options.B: Code reuse through libraries, which simplifies program creation and ensures both apps benefit from the same tested payment logic
options.C: Iteration, because payment processing involves repeating steps
options.D: Nested conditionals, because payment validation involves multiple conditions

questions.explanation: The use of libraries simplifies the task of creating complex programs. Both programmers reusing the same payment library demonstrates code reuse — a key benefit of libraries.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the relationship between libraries and procedural abstraction?

options.A: Libraries and procedural abstraction are unrelated concepts
options.B: Libraries are collections of procedures that embody procedural abstraction — users call library procedures knowing what they do without needing to know how they work
options.C: Libraries replace the need for procedural abstraction because they handle all complexity
options.D: Procedural abstraction is only used when libraries are not available

questions.explanation: Libraries contain procedures that embody procedural abstraction. When a programmer uses a library procedure, they use it knowing only what it does (its behavior as described in the API), not how it is implemented internally.

questions.question: A programmer uses a library without reading its documentation and calls a procedure with incorrect arguments. Which of the following best explains this outcome?

options.A: This is expected behavior because libraries should work with any arguments
options.B: Documentation for an API/library is necessary to understand how to use the procedures correctly, and not reading it can lead to errors
options.C: The library should have automatically corrected the arguments
options.D: This is the library creator's fault for not making the procedure more flexible

questions.explanation: Documentation for an API/library is necessary in understanding the behaviors provided by the API/library and how to use them. Without reading the documentation, a programmer may call procedures incorrectly.

questions.question: Which TWO of the following are true about software libraries and APIs?

options.A: A software library contains procedures that may be used in creating new programs
options.B: An API is a physical device that connects different software programs
options.C: Documentation for an API is necessary to understand the behaviors provided and how to use them
options.D: Libraries guarantee that programs using them will never contain bugs

questions.explanation: A software library contains procedures for use in creating new programs (A). API documentation is necessary to understand behaviors and usage (C). An API is a specification, not a physical device (B is false). Libraries do not guarantee bug-free programs (D is false).

questions.question: What does RANDOM(1, 6) return?

options.A: Always 1
options.B: Always 6
options.C: A random integer from 1 to 6 inclusive, with each result equally likely
options.D: A random decimal between 1 and 6

questions.explanation: RANDOM(a, b) generates and returns a random integer from a to b inclusive. Each result is equally likely to occur. RANDOM(1, 6) could return 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6.

questions.question: A programmer runs the same program twice. The program contains RANDOM(1, 100). Which of the following best describes what happens?

options.A: Both runs produce the same result because RANDOM always returns the same value
options.B: Each execution may produce a different result because random number generation means each run can produce a different value
options.C: The second run always produces a higher number than the first run
options.D: RANDOM produces an error if called more than once in the same program

questions.explanation: Using random number generation in a program means each execution may produce a different result. This is a key characteristic of programs that use RANDOM.

questions.question: Which of the following could be a result of RANDOM(3, 7)?
questions.explanation: RANDOM(3, 7) generates a random integer from 3 to 7 inclusive. Possible results: 3, 4, 5, 6, or 7. 2 is below the range, 8 is above the range, and 3.5 is not an integer.

questions.question: A programmer wants to simulate rolling a standard 6-sided die. Which of the following correctly implements this?

options.A: RANDOM(0, 6)
options.B: RANDOM(1, 6)
options.C: RANDOM(1, 7)
options.D: RANDOM(0, 5)

questions.explanation: A standard die produces values 1 through 6 inclusive. RANDOM(1, 6) generates a random integer from 1 to 6 inclusive, correctly simulating a die roll.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the probability of displaying 'heads'?

options.A: It is impossible to display 'heads'
options.B: There is a 25% chance of displaying 'heads'
options.C: There is a 50% chance of displaying 'heads'
options.D: There is a 75% chance of displaying 'heads'

questions.explanation: RANDOM(1, 4) returns 1, 2, 3, or 4 each with equal probability (25% each). 'Heads' only displays when result = 1, which has a 1/4 = 25% probability.

questions.question: How many possible values can RANDOM(5, 10) return?
questions.explanation: RANDOM(5, 10) returns a random integer from 5 to 10 inclusive. The possible values are 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 — that is 6 possible values.

questions.question: A programmer wants to randomly select an element from a list aList that has 8 elements. Which of the following correctly generates a valid random index?

options.A: RANDOM(0, 8)
options.B: RANDOM(0, 7)
options.C: RANDOM(1, 8)
options.D: RANDOM(1, 9)

questions.explanation: In AP CSP, list indices start at 1 and go up to the length of the list. For a list with 8 elements, valid indices are 1 through 8. RANDOM(1, 8) generates a valid random index.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the expected output of this code segment?

options.A: Always exactly 0
options.B: Always exactly 100
options.C: Always exactly 16 or 17
options.D: A value that varies each run, expected to be approximately 1/6 of 100 (around 16-17)

questions.explanation: Using random number generation means each execution may produce a different result. Each roll has a 1/6 chance of being 6, so out of 100 rolls approximately 16-17 are expected to be 6, but the exact count varies each run.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly generates a random even number between 2 and 10 inclusive?

options.A: RANDOM(2, 10)
options.B: RANDOM(1, 5) * 2
options.C: RANDOM(2, 10) * 2
options.D: RANDOM(0, 4) + 2

questions.explanation: RANDOM(1, 5) generates 1, 2, 3, 4, or 5. Multiplying by 2 gives 2, 4, 6, 8, or 10 — all even numbers between 2 and 10 inclusive. RANDOM(2, 10) would generate odd numbers too.

questions.question: A programmer claims that running the same program with RANDOM multiple times should always produce the same output to make testing easier. Which of the following best evaluates this claim?

options.A: The claim is correct — programs should always produce the same output for consistency
options.B: The claim is incorrect — using random number generation means each execution may produce a different result, which is the intended behavior for programs that need randomness
options.C: The claim is correct because RANDOM always returns the same value within a single run
options.D: The claim is incorrect because RANDOM values should decrease with each run

questions.explanation: Using random number generation in a program means each execution may produce a different result. This is the intended behavior — if reproducibility is needed for testing, a fixed seed can be used, but random programs are expected to vary.

questions.question: What does RANDOM(10, 10) return?

options.A: A random integer between 0 and 10
options.B: Always 10, because the range contains only one value
options.C: An error because a and b must be different
options.D: 0, because 10 - 10 = 0

questions.explanation: RANDOM(a, b) generates a random integer from a to b inclusive. When a = b = 10, the only possible value is 10. It always returns 10.

questions.question: A programmer uses RANDOM to simulate flipping a coin — RANDOM(1, 2) where 1 = heads and 2 = tails. Which of the following best describes each result's probability?

options.A: Heads has a 75% chance and tails has a 25% chance
options.B: Heads has a 50% chance and tails has a 50% chance
options.C: The probability changes with each flip based on previous results
options.D: Both values have equal probability only on the first flip

questions.explanation: RANDOM generates values with each result equally likely to occur. RANDOM(1, 2) produces 1 or 2 each with 50% probability — a fair coin flip simulation.

questions.question: A programmer wants to generate a random number between 0 and 1 inclusive. Which of the following best describes a limitation of RANDOM in AP CSP?

options.A: RANDOM cannot generate the value 0
options.B: RANDOM only generates integers, so it cannot directly generate 0.5 or other decimals between 0 and 1
options.C: RANDOM can only generate numbers between 1 and 100
options.D: RANDOM always generates the same value when called with the same arguments

questions.explanation: RANDOM(a, b) generates a random integer from a to b inclusive. Since it only generates integers, it cannot directly produce decimal values like 0.5, 0.3, etc. between 0 and 1.

questions.question: Which of the following expressions generates a random integer from 1 to 100 inclusive?

options.A: RANDOM(0, 99)
options.B: RANDOM(1, 99)
options.C: RANDOM(1, 100)
options.D: RANDOM(0, 100)

questions.explanation: RANDOM(1, 100) generates a random integer from 1 to 100 inclusive — exactly the range required. RANDOM(0, 100) includes 0 which is outside the desired range.

questions.question: Which TWO of the following are true about the RANDOM function in AP CSP?

options.A: RANDOM(a, b) generates a random integer from a to b inclusive
options.B: RANDOM always produces the same sequence of values each time the program runs
options.C: Each possible result of RANDOM is equally likely to occur
options.D: RANDOM can generate decimal values between its two arguments

questions.explanation: RANDOM generates a random integer from a to b inclusive (A), and each result is equally likely (C). Using RANDOM means each execution may produce a different result (B is false). RANDOM generates integers only, not decimals (D is false).

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a simulation?

options.A: A program that displays real-time data from sensors in the physical world
options.B: An abstraction of a more complex object or phenomenon for a specific purpose
options.C: A program that stores and retrieves data from a database
options.D: An algorithm that solves a problem in the most efficient way possible

questions.explanation: Simulations are abstractions of more complex objects or phenomena for a specific purpose. They use varying sets of values to reflect the changing state of a phenomenon.

questions.question: Researchers have developed a simulation of packets traveling between computers in a network. Which of the following are most likely to be results of running the simulation? Select the best answer.

options.A: Better understanding of the effect of temporarily unavailable network connections AND better understanding of the impact of increased connection speeds
options.B: Better understanding of how to physically install network cables AND better understanding of packet encryption
options.C: Better understanding of the effect of using binary data AND better understanding of user interface design
options.D: Better understanding of how to purchase network equipment AND better understanding of ISP pricing

questions.explanation: Simulations allow investigation of a phenomenon without the constraints of the real world and facilitate formulation of hypotheses. A network packet simulation would most likely give insight into how connection availability and speeds affect packet transmission.

questions.question: Which of the following is the BEST reason to use a simulation instead of a real-world experiment?

options.A: Simulations always produce more accurate results than real-world experiments
options.B: Simulations are most useful when real-world events are impractical for experiments such as when they are too big, too small, too fast, too slow, too expensive, or too dangerous
options.C: Simulations can only be used when real-world experiments are impossible
options.D: Simulations are always cheaper than real-world experiments

questions.explanation: Simulations are most useful when real-world events are impractical for experiments — too big, too small, too fast, too slow, too expensive, or too dangerous. They allow investigation without the constraints of the real world.

questions.question: A scientist creates a simulation of a hurricane to predict its path and intensity. The simulation leaves out factors like ocean current temperature variations at depths below 100 meters. Which of the following best describes this limitation?

options.A: The simulation is invalid because it does not include all real-world factors
options.B: The process of developing a simulation involves removing specific details or simplifying functionality which may affect accuracy
options.C: The simulation should be replaced with a real hurricane for more accurate results
options.D: Simulations of weather events are always more accurate than real-world observation

questions.explanation: The process of developing an abstract simulation involves removing specific details or simplifying functionality. Omitting ocean depth temperature variations is a simplification that may affect the simulation's accuracy.

questions.question: A car company uses a simulation to test how a new airbag design performs in a crash. Why is simulation particularly appropriate here?

options.A: Crash testing is too slow to do in real life
options.B: Crash testing is too dangerous and expensive to perform repeatedly in the real world — simulation allows investigation without these constraints
options.C: Computer simulations are always more accurate than physical crash tests
options.D: Real crash tests cannot measure the forces involved

questions.explanation: Simulations are most useful when real-world events are impractical — in this case, too dangerous and expensive. Simulations allow investigation of the airbag design without the constraints of the real world.

questions.question: A climate simulation predicts that global temperatures will rise by 2°C by 2100. The simulation was built by a team that only included data from the Northern Hemisphere. Which of the following best describes a potential problem with this simulation?

options.A: The simulation is invalid because climate cannot be simulated on a computer
options.B: Simulations can contain bias derived from the choices of real-world elements that were included or excluded
options.C: The prediction is definitely wrong because simulations cannot predict the future
options.D: The simulation should use more random number generation to account for variability

questions.explanation: Simulations can contain bias derived from the choices of real-world elements that were included or excluded. Excluding Southern Hemisphere data introduces bias into the climate simulation.

questions.question: Why are random number generators used in simulations?

options.A: To make simulations run faster by skipping unnecessary calculations
options.B: To simulate the variability that exists in the real world
options.C: To ensure that simulations always produce the same result for reproducibility
options.D: To replace real-world data that is unavailable to the researchers

questions.explanation: Random number generators can be used to simulate the variability that exists in the real world. Real-world phenomena are rarely perfectly predictable, and random values introduce the natural variation found in reality.

questions.question: A researcher uses a simulation to study the spread of a disease through a population. After running the simulation, they form a hypothesis about which interventions would be most effective. Which of the following best describes this use of simulation?

options.A: The simulation proves which interventions will definitely work
options.B: Simulations facilitate the formulation and refinement of hypotheses related to the objects or phenomena under consideration
options.C: The researcher is misusing simulation because disease spread should only be studied with real data
options.D: The simulation replaces the need for any real-world testing of interventions

questions.explanation: Simulations facilitate the formulation and refinement of hypotheses related to the objects or phenomena under consideration. Using simulation to form hypotheses about disease interventions is a key application of simulation.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of using a simulation because the real-world event is too small?

options.A: Simulating traffic flow in a city to test new traffic light timing
options.B: Simulating atomic interactions to study chemical reactions at the molecular level
options.C: Simulating stock market behavior to test investment strategies
options.D: Simulating weather patterns to predict next week's weather

questions.explanation: Simulations are most useful when real-world events are impractical — including when they are too small to observe directly. Atomic and molecular interactions are too small to observe directly, making simulation the practical approach.

questions.question: A simulation of a forest fire excludes wind patterns because they are difficult to model. A student argues this makes the simulation completely useless. Which of the following best evaluates this argument?

options.A: The student is correct — a simulation missing any real-world factor is useless
options.B: The student is incorrect — simulations involve removing specific details or simplifying functionality and can still provide useful insights even without modeling every factor
options.C: The student is correct — only perfectly accurate simulations should be used
options.D: The student is incorrect because wind patterns never affect forest fire spread

questions.explanation: The process of developing an abstract simulation involves removing specific details or simplifying functionality. Simulations do not need to be perfect to be useful — they provide insight even without modeling every real-world factor.

questions.question: How does a simulation reflect the changing state of a phenomenon?

options.A: By connecting to live sensors that measure the real phenomenon in real time
options.B: By using varying sets of values that change as the simulation progresses to model how the phenomenon evolves
options.C: By taking a single snapshot of the phenomenon at one point in time
options.D: By averaging past measurements and displaying a single fixed value

questions.explanation: A simulation is a representation that uses varying sets of values to reflect the changing state of a phenomenon. As the simulation runs, these values change to model how the real-world phenomenon would evolve over time.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a simulation being used because the real-world event is too slow?

options.A: Simulating a nuclear explosion to study its effects
options.B: Simulating millions of years of geological change to study how mountains form
options.C: Simulating a car crash to test safety features
options.D: Simulating stock market trading to test investment algorithms

questions.explanation: Simulations are most useful when real-world events are impractical — including when too slow. Geological changes that take millions of years cannot be directly observed on human timescales, making simulation the only practical approach.

questions.question: A simulation of traffic in a city models cars as identical objects that all move at exactly the speed limit. In reality, drivers have different speeds and driving behaviors. Which of the following best describes this simplification?

options.A: This is an error that makes the simulation invalid
options.B: This is an abstraction where specific details are removed to simplify functionality, which may introduce some inaccuracy but makes the simulation feasible to build
options.C: This is appropriate because all drivers do follow the speed limit
options.D: This demonstrates bias because the simulation excludes reckless drivers

questions.explanation: The process of developing an abstract simulation involves removing specific details or simplifying functionality. Modeling all cars as identical is a simplification that trades accuracy for tractability.

questions.question: A teacher uses a simulation to demonstrate what would happen if a large asteroid hit Earth. Which of the following best justifies using a simulation rather than observing the real event?

options.A: The simulation will produce the exact same results as a real asteroid impact
options.B: A real asteroid impact would be too dangerous and impossible to stage — simulation allows investigation without the constraints of the real world
options.C: The simulation is more educational than a real event would be
options.D: Real asteroid impacts happen too frequently to wait for one to occur

questions.explanation: Simulations are most useful when real-world events are impractical — in this case, too dangerous and impossible to stage. Simulation allows investigation of asteroid impacts without real-world constraints.

questions.question: Which TWO of the following are potential limitations of simulations?

options.A: Simulations can contain bias from real-world elements that were included or excluded
options.B: Simulations always produce the exact same results as real-world experiments
options.C: Developing a simulation involves removing specific details or simplifying functionality which may affect accuracy
options.D: Simulations can only be run once before they need to be rebuilt

questions.explanation: Simulations can contain bias from choices of what to include or exclude (A), and developing a simulation involves removing details or simplifying functionality which may affect results (C). Simulations do not always match real-world results exactly (B is false). Simulations can be run multiple times (D is false).

questions.question: Which of the following best describes algorithmic efficiency?

options.A: How accurately an algorithm produces correct output
options.B: An estimation of the amount of computational resources used by an algorithm
options.C: The number of lines of code in an algorithm
options.D: How readable and well-documented an algorithm is

questions.explanation: Algorithmic efficiency is an estimation of the amount of computational resources used by an algorithm. This is typically measured as a function of the size of the input.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a problem with reasonable running time?

options.A: A problem that can be solved in exactly 1 second
options.B: A problem whose solution has polynomial efficiency or lower (constant, linear, square, cube, etc.)
options.C: A problem that requires exponential or factorial time to solve
options.D: A problem that can only be solved by a supercomputer

questions.explanation: A problem is considered to have a reasonable running time if it can be solved with polynomial efficiency or lower (constant, linear, square, cube, etc.). Exponential and factorial time algorithms are considered unreasonable.

questions.question: What is a heuristic approach to a problem?

options.A: An approach that guarantees finding the optimal solution to any problem
options.B: An approach that produces a solution not guaranteed to be optimal but may be used when finding an optimal solution is impractical
options.C: A mathematical proof that a problem cannot be solved
options.D: An approach that converts an undecidable problem into a decidable one

questions.explanation: A heuristic approach produces a solution that is not guaranteed to be optimal but may be used when techniques that are guaranteed to find an optimal solution are impractical due to unreasonable running time.

questions.question: What is the difference between a decision problem and an optimization problem?

options.A: Decision problems are harder than optimization problems
options.B: A decision problem has a yes/no answer while an optimization problem seeks to find the best solution among many possibilities
options.C: Optimization problems always have reasonable running time while decision problems do not
options.D: Decision problems can only be solved by humans while optimization problems can be solved by computers

questions.explanation: A decision problem is one with a yes or no answer. An optimization problem has the goal of finding the best solution. For example, 'Is there a path from A to B?' is a decision problem, while 'What is the shortest path from A to B?' is an optimization problem.

questions.question: A programmer informally measures the efficiency of an algorithm by counting how many times a specific statement executes as the input size increases. Which of the following best describes this approach?

options.A: This is an invalid measurement because only formal mathematical proofs can measure efficiency
options.B: Algorithmic efficiency can be informally measured by determining the number of times a statement or group of statements executes
options.C: This only measures the memory usage of the algorithm, not its time efficiency
options.D: This approach only works for algorithms with REPEAT n TIMES loops

questions.explanation: Algorithmic efficiency can be informally measured by determining the number of times a statement or group of statements executes. This gives an estimate of how computational resources scale with input size.

questions.question: Which of the following types of algorithmic efficiency is considered UNREASONABLE?

options.A: Linear efficiency
options.B: Square efficiency
options.C: Exponential efficiency
options.D: Cubic efficiency

questions.explanation: Exponential efficiency is considered unreasonable. Reasonable efficiency includes polynomial types (constant, linear, square, cube, etc.). Exponential and factorial efficiency are unreasonable because they grow too quickly for large inputs.

questions.question: A programmer is trying to solve the traveling salesman problem (find the shortest route visiting all cities exactly once). The exact solution has exponential running time. The programmer uses an approximate algorithm that finds a good (but not necessarily shortest) route quickly. Which of the following best describes this approach?

options.A: The programmer is making an error because only exact solutions are acceptable
options.B: The programmer is using a heuristic — an approach that produces a solution not guaranteed to be optimal but used when finding the optimal solution is impractical
options.C: The programmer is using binary search to find the optimal route
options.D: The programmer is solving an undecidable problem

questions.explanation: When a problem cannot be solved in reasonable time, heuristics are used to find approximate solutions. A heuristic produces a solution not guaranteed to be optimal but may be used when optimal solutions are impractical due to unreasonable running time.

questions.question: Algorithm A solves a problem in a number of steps equal to n (linear). Algorithm B solves the same problem in n² steps (quadratic). Which of the following best describes the efficiency comparison for large values of n?

options.A: Algorithm A is more efficient because it uses fewer steps
options.B: Algorithm B is more efficient because squaring makes numbers larger which means more work gets done
options.C: Both algorithms have the same efficiency because they solve the same problem
options.D: Neither algorithm is efficient — only algorithms with constant time are acceptable

questions.explanation: Algorithm A with linear efficiency (n steps) is more efficient than Algorithm B with quadratic efficiency (n² steps). Different algorithms can be developed to solve the same problem and they can have different efficiencies. For large n, n steps is much fewer than n² steps.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a decision problem?

options.A: What is the maximum profit achievable from a set of investments?
options.B: What is the shortest path between two cities?
options.C: Is it possible to color a map using only 4 colors so that no two adjacent regions share a color?
options.D: Which item in a list has the highest value?

questions.explanation: A decision problem is one with a yes or no answer. 'Is it possible to color a map using only 4 colors?' has a yes/no answer. The other options seek to find a best value or path, making them optimization problems.

questions.question: A problem requires checking every possible combination of n items. The number of combinations grows as 2ⁿ (doubles with each new item). Which of the following best classifies this algorithm?

options.A: Reasonable running time because the growth is predictable
options.B: Unreasonable running time because exponential efficiency grows too quickly for large n
options.C: Reasonable running time because the algorithm works correctly for all inputs
options.D: Unreasonable running time only when n is odd

questions.explanation: Exponential efficiency (2ⁿ) is considered unreasonable. Problems with exponential running time become impractical to solve even for moderately large values of n because the number of steps grows too quickly.

questions.question: Some problems cannot be solved in a reasonable amount of time. In these cases, what do programmers typically seek instead of an optimal solution?

options.A: A solution that runs in exactly polynomial time
options.B: A solution that is completely random to approximate the optimal answer
options.C: An approximate solution using a heuristic approach
options.D: No solution because the problem should be abandoned

questions.explanation: Some problems cannot be solved in a reasonable amount of time. In these cases, approximate solutions are sought using heuristic approaches that produce good but not necessarily optimal solutions.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the relationship between input size and efficiency?

options.A: Efficiency is unrelated to input size — an efficient algorithm runs fast regardless of input
options.B: Algorithmic efficiency is typically expressed as a function of the size of the input — as input grows, the number of steps the algorithm takes changes accordingly
options.C: Larger inputs always make algorithms more efficient because there is more data to work with
options.D: Input size only affects efficiency for sorting algorithms

questions.explanation: Algorithmic efficiency is typically expressed as a function of the size of the input. As input size grows, the number of steps required changes — linear algorithms add steps proportionally, quadratic algorithms add steps squared, etc.

questions.question: Two algorithms solve the same problem. Algorithm A uses 3n steps and Algorithm B uses n² steps. For n = 10, which is more efficient and by how much?

options.A: Algorithm A: 30 steps vs Algorithm B: 100 steps — Algorithm A is more efficient
options.B: Algorithm A: 30 steps vs Algorithm B: 20 steps — Algorithm B is more efficient
options.C: Algorithm A: 300 steps vs Algorithm B: 100 steps — Algorithm B is more efficient
options.D: Both use the same number of steps for n = 10

questions.explanation: For n = 10: Algorithm A uses 3(10) = 30 steps. Algorithm B uses 10² = 100 steps. Algorithm A is more efficient, using 30 steps compared to 100 steps. Different algorithms solving the same problem can have different efficiencies.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes why adding more computing power does not always solve problems with unreasonable running time?

options.A: More computing power always makes any algorithm fast enough
options.B: Exponential and factorial algorithms grow so quickly that even with more computing power, they remain impractical for large inputs because the number of steps grows faster than hardware improvements can compensate
options.C: More computing power only helps with memory-intensive algorithms, not time-intensive ones
options.D: Unreasonable running time only applies to algorithms with fewer than 100 steps

questions.explanation: Problems with unreasonable (exponential or factorial) running time grow so quickly that even doubling or tripling computing power only marginally increases the size of problems that can be solved. The fundamental inefficiency cannot be overcome by hardware alone.

questions.question: Which TWO of the following are classified as REASONABLE running times?

options.A: Linear efficiency (n steps)
options.B: Exponential efficiency (2ⁿ steps)
options.C: Quadratic efficiency (n² steps)
options.D: Factorial efficiency (n! steps)

questions.explanation: Reasonable running times include polynomial efficiency or lower: constant, linear (n), quadratic (n²), cubic (n³), etc. Exponential (2ⁿ) and factorial (n!) are unreasonable because they grow too quickly for large inputs.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a decidable problem?

options.A: A problem that can be solved in polynomial time
options.B: A decision problem for which an algorithm can be written to produce a correct yes or no answer for all inputs
options.C: A problem that has exactly one correct solution
options.D: A problem that can be solved by a heuristic approach

questions.explanation: A decidable problem is a decision problem for which an algorithm can be written that is always capable of producing a correct yes or no answer.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes an undecidable problem?

options.A: A problem that takes too long to solve but eventually produces an answer
options.B: A problem for which no algorithm can be constructed that is always capable of providing a correct yes or no answer
options.C: A problem that can only be solved by quantum computers
options.D: A problem that requires human judgment and cannot be automated

questions.explanation: An undecidable problem is one for which no algorithm can be constructed that is always capable of providing a correct yes or no answer. It is not that we haven't found the algorithm yet — it is proven that no such algorithm can exist.

questions.question: The Halting Problem asks: 'Given a program and its input, will the program eventually stop running?' This is a famous example of an undecidable problem. Which of the following best describes what this means?

options.A: Some programs are too large to analyze so we cannot determine if they halt
options.B: No algorithm can be written that correctly determines whether any arbitrary program will halt or run forever for all possible inputs
options.C: The Halting Problem can be solved for most programs but not all
options.D: The Halting Problem is too difficult for current computers but will be solvable by future ones

questions.explanation: An undecidable problem is one for which no algorithm can be constructed that is always capable of providing a correct yes or no answer. For the Halting Problem, it has been proven mathematically that no such algorithm can exist for all possible programs and inputs.

questions.question: A student claims that the question 'Is the integer n evenly divisible by 3?' is undecidable because some numbers are very large. Which of the following best evaluates this claim?

options.A: The claim is correct — very large numbers make the problem undecidable
options.B: The claim is incorrect — this is a decidable problem because an algorithm (checking if n MOD 3 = 0) can always produce a correct yes or no answer for any integer
options.C: The claim is correct — divisibility problems are always undecidable
options.D: The claim is correct because the algorithm might run for too long on large numbers

questions.explanation: This is a decidable problem. An algorithm can always determine if n MOD 3 = 0 and produce a correct yes or no answer for any integer. A problem being difficult or slow does not make it undecidable — undecidability means no correct algorithm can exist.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the key distinction between a problem being undecidable versus just having an unreasonable running time?

options.A: Undecidable problems take too long to solve while problems with unreasonable running time are impossible to solve
options.B: Problems with unreasonable running time can be solved by an algorithm eventually — they just take too long. Undecidable problems have no algorithm that can always produce a correct answer, regardless of time
options.C: They are the same thing — undecidable problems and unreasonable running time both mean the problem cannot be solved
options.D: Undecidable problems only apply to optimization problems while unreasonable running time applies to decision problems

questions.explanation: These are distinct concepts. An algorithm with unreasonable running time can still produce a correct answer — it just takes too long. An undecidable problem has no algorithm that can always produce a correct answer, no matter how much time is given.

questions.question: An undecidable problem may have some instances with algorithmic solutions. Which of the following best explains this?

options.A: If some instances can be solved, the problem is actually decidable
options.B: An undecidable problem may have some instances with solutions but no single algorithm can solve all instances — the undecidability refers to the general case
options.C: Instances that can be solved should be separated into a new decidable problem
options.D: Undecidable problems can never have any solvable instances

questions.explanation: An undecidable problem may have some instances with an algorithmic solution, but no single algorithm can solve all instances. The undecidability is about whether a general algorithm exists that works for all inputs.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a decidable problem?

options.A: Determining whether a given program will halt for all possible inputs
options.B: Determining whether a given integer is prime
options.C: Determining whether a given program is free of all bugs
options.D: Determining whether a given program will produce correct output for all possible inputs

questions.explanation: Determining whether an integer is prime is decidable — an algorithm (checking divisibility up to the square root) can always produce a correct yes or no answer. The Halting Problem (A) and verifying program correctness (C, D) are undecidable.

questions.question: A computer scientist proves that a new problem P cannot be solved by any algorithm for all possible inputs. Which of the following best classifies problem P?

options.A: P is a problem with unreasonable running time
options.B: P is an undecidable problem
options.C: P is a heuristic problem
options.D: P is an optimization problem

questions.explanation: An undecidable problem is one for which no algorithm can be constructed that is always capable of providing a correct yes or no answer. If it is proven no algorithm exists for all inputs, the problem is undecidable.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes why the existence of undecidable problems is significant?

options.A: It means computers will eventually become powerful enough to solve these problems
options.B: It establishes fundamental limits on what can be computed — there are problems for which no algorithm can ever be written to always produce a correct answer
options.C: It means programmers need to write better algorithms to solve these problems
options.D: It only affects theoretical computer science and has no practical implications

questions.explanation: The existence of undecidable problems establishes fundamental limits on computation. There are inherent boundaries to what can be computed — these are not engineering limitations that better hardware or algorithms can overcome.

questions.question: A programmer writes an algorithm that correctly determines whether a specific program with a specific input halts. Does this contradict the undecidability of the Halting Problem?

options.A: Yes — if one instance is solvable, the Halting Problem must be decidable
options.B: No — an undecidable problem may have some instances with an algorithmic solution, but no single algorithm can solve ALL instances
options.C: Yes — this proves the Halting Problem is actually decidable
options.D: No — because the programmer's algorithm must have an error

questions.explanation: An undecidable problem may have some instances with an algorithmic solution, but no single algorithm can solve all instances. Solving one specific case does not make the general problem decidable.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the difference between decidable and undecidable problems?

options.A: Decidable problems can be solved quickly while undecidable problems take too long
options.B: Decidable problems have algorithms that always produce a correct answer for all inputs while undecidable problems have no such algorithm
options.C: Decidable problems have yes/no answers while undecidable problems have numerical answers
options.D: Decidable problems are always optimization problems while undecidable problems are always decision problems

questions.explanation: A decidable problem has an algorithm that can always produce a correct yes or no answer for all inputs. An undecidable problem has no such algorithm — it is not about speed but about the fundamental impossibility of a general solution.

questions.question: A student says that undecidable problems will be solvable once quantum computers are powerful enough. Which of the following best evaluates this statement?

options.A: The student is correct — quantum computers can solve problems that classical computers cannot
options.B: The student is incorrect — undecidability is a mathematical property that means no algorithm can exist, regardless of the computing power or type of computer used
options.C: The student is correct — quantum computers have already solved some undecidable problems
options.D: The student is partially correct — quantum computers can solve undecidable problems if given enough time

questions.explanation: Undecidability is not about computing power — it is a mathematical property proven to mean that no algorithm (on any type of computer) can always produce a correct answer. More powerful computers cannot overcome fundamental mathematical impossibility.

questions.question: Which of the following is the best example of a decidable problem?

options.A: Determining whether a program will run forever given any input
options.B: Determining the shortest path between two points
options.C: Determining whether a given number is even or odd
options.D: Determining whether a program is free of all security vulnerabilities

questions.explanation: Determining whether a number is even or odd is decidable — an algorithm (check num MOD 2) can always produce a correct yes or no answer for any integer. The halting problem (A) and general program verification (D) are undecidable. Finding shortest path (B) is an optimization problem, not a decision problem.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes why some undecidable problems still have practical value despite being undecidable?

options.A: They are undecidable only in theory — in practice they can always be solved
options.B: An undecidable problem may have some instances with algorithmic solutions, and heuristics can produce useful approximate answers even when a general solution does not exist
options.C: Undecidable problems have no practical value because they cannot be solved
options.D: Undecidable problems become decidable when the input size is small enough

questions.explanation: An undecidable problem may have some instances with algorithmic solutions, and heuristics can produce useful approximate answers. Even though no general algorithm exists, partial solutions and approximations can still be practically valuable.

questions.question: Which TWO of the following are true about undecidable problems?

options.A: No algorithm can be constructed that always produces a correct yes or no answer for all inputs
options.B: Undecidable problems will eventually be solved as computers become more powerful
options.C: An undecidable problem may have some specific instances that can be solved algorithmically
options.D: Undecidable problems are the same as problems with unreasonable running time

questions.explanation: No algorithm can always produce a correct answer for all inputs of an undecidable problem (A). However, an undecidable problem may have some instances with algorithmic solutions (C). More computing power cannot solve undecidable problems (B is false). Undecidability and unreasonable running time are distinct concepts (D is false).

questions.question:

questions.rubric:

questions.stimulus: A programmer has a sorted list of 1,000 student ID numbers and needs to determine whether a specific ID is in the list.
questions.question:
Part A: The programmer is deciding between linear search and binary search. Identify which algorithm would be more efficient for this task and explain why.

Part B: Describe what the binary search algorithm does. Explain the requirement necessary to use binary search on this list.
questions.rubric:
PART A (2 points):
Award 1 point for correctly identifying binary search as more efficient.
Award 1 point for explaining that binary search eliminates half the remaining data with each step making it much faster than linear search which checks elements one at a time on large sorted data sets.

PART B (2 points):
Award 1 point for describing binary search: it starts at the middle of the sorted data set, eliminates half the data based on whether the target is higher or lower, and repeats until the value is found or all elements are eliminated.
Award 1 point for stating the requirement: the data must be in sorted order to use binary search.
